contributions: GrACE, a generative confidence-elicitation method that produces a discriminative and calibrated confidence score during generation itself (via similarity to a learned special-token embedding), eliminating the separate post-generation evaluation stage and auxiliary-model overhead that prior methods require
a k-fold-binning procedure for constructing smooth, accuracy-aligned calibration targets from an uncalibrated linear-probe confidence score, improving on binary-label calibration training

two confidence-weighted test-time-scaling strategies (GrACE-SC, GrACE-ES) that integrate GrACE's real-time confidence into self-consistency voting and early-stopping, improving accuracy while substantially reducing the number of samples required at inference

empirical results showing GrACE outperforms six confidence-elicitation baselines on calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, AUROC) on open-ended generation, generalizes better than trained baselines under domain shift, and produces confidence that drives TTS more effectively than P(True) or verbalized confidence
limitations: GrACE provides only a single confidence score reflecting overall confidence for the entire generation; it cannot give separate confidence scores for every claim in the response or for each individual step in a chain-of-thought, which the authors flag as future work. GrACE focuses only on reflecting the factuality of a response through confidence, while other quality dimensions such as completeness are not addressed and are left for future work. GrACE only assesses model confidence but does not itself improve the model's underlying confidence or correctness.
method: GrACE (Generative cAlibrated Confidence Elicitation) adds a special token <CNF> to the model's vocabulary and fine-tunes the model to append it at the end of every response; confidence is then computed, with no extra forward pass or auxiliary model, as the similarity between the last-layer hidden state at the <CNF> position and <CNF>'s learned embedding (softmax over the vocabulary at that position, read off at the <CNF> slot) -- leveraging the same generation mechanism the LM head already uses to project hidden states onto vocabulary similarity. To set well-calibrated training targets, a linear probe is first trained (via k-fold cross-validation) to predict an uncalibrated confidence score from the last hidden state for every training sample; samples are grouped into bins by this probed score, and each sample's calibration target is set to the empirical accuracy of its bin, producing calibration targets that are numerically aligned with actual correctness rates rather than binary 0/1 labels. The model is then fine-tuned (LoRA on <CNF>'s embedding, plus the base model) with a combined loss: a calibration MSE loss between the <CNF>-derived confidence and this binned target, plus a standard SFT loss on the original response (excluding <CNF> from the SFT loss) as a regularizer to prevent the calibration objective from degrading generation quality. Building on this real-time confidence signal, two test-time-scaling strategies are introduced: GrACE-SC (Self-Consistency with GrACE) replaces plain majority voting with confidence-weighted voting, giving higher-confidence samples more influence in the final answer selection; GrACE-ES (Early Stopping with GrACE) halts sampling as soon as any generated sample's confidence exceeds a threshold tau, falling back to GrACE-SC if the budget is exhausted without reaching that threshold. Evaluated on open-ended generation calibration (TriviaQA, SciQ; Phi3-3.8B, Llama2-7B, Llama3.1-8B backbones) against six baselines (Seq. Likelihood, Platt Scaling, P(True), Verbal, Apricot, ActCab) via ECE/Brier/AUROC, and on test-time scaling (MathQA, ARC_Challenge; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) against Self-Consistency, Adaptive Self-Consistency (ASC), and Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC).
methods: Seq. Likelihood / Platt Scaling / P(True) / Verbal / Apricot / ActCab (baselines)
one_liner: GrACE teaches an LLM to output a discriminative, calibrated confidence score during generation itself -- via the similarity between the last hidden state and a learned embedding for a special <CNF> token, trained against k-fold-binned accuracy targets -- eliminating the separate evaluation stage post-generation methods require, and uses this on-the-fly confidence to weight self-consistency voting and drive early-stopping, improving test-time-scaling accuracy by up to 3.3% while cutting required samples by more than half in many cases.
problem: Assessing LLM reliability via confidence elicitation is central to safe deployment and to test-time scaling, but existing approaches either require an expensive additional post-generation evaluation stage (increasing latency, often needing an auxiliary model) or use verbalized confidence, which is vague, poorly standardized/quantifiable across expressions ('most likely' vs. 'likely'), and empirically overconfident, making both approaches impractical or unreliable for real-time, on-the-fly deployment.

relevance.overthinking: Directly relevant as an efficiency mechanism for test-time scaling: GrACE-ES's confidence-thresholded early stopping is a concrete inference-time method for avoiding wasted sampling once the model is reliably confident, cutting required samples by more than half in easier settings (80.1% of ARC_C queries need only one sample) while improving accuracy -- directly addressing the same 'don't spend more compute than the problem needs' principle central to overthinking mitigation, but applied to the outer sampling loop (how many parallel attempts to generate) rather than to reasoning-trace token length within a single generation. Its finding that miscalibrated confidence (overconfident verbalized scores, underconfident P(True)) directly causes either premature termination on wrong answers or wasted budget on easy ones is a clear demonstration of why calibration quality -- not just having some confidence signal -- is load-bearing for any confidence-driven overthinking or budget-control mechanism.

results: On open-ended generation calibration, GrACE achieves the best AUROC among all seven methods on 5 of 6 backbone/dataset combinations and outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method (Apricot) by 3.9%, 2.5%, and 5.0% in ECE, Brier, and AUROC on average, while leaving accuracy unaffected (fine-tuning with the calibration loss does not degrade generation quality). Cross-domain generalization (train on TriviaQA/SciQ, test on the other) shows GrACE has the strongest generalization of the three trainable methods tested, with only marginal ECE (+3.3%) and Brier (+2.4%) increases and a small AUROC drop (-3.9%) under domain shift, while Apricot's AUROC degrades 16.0% on average under the same shift -- attributed to Apricot relying more on question-semantics shortcuts that transfer poorly, whereas GrACE explicitly teaches the LLM itself the correctness-probability distribution rather than only training an external linear probe (ActCab), which cannot fully capture the question-answer correspondence. For test-time scaling at a fixed sampling budget of 8, GrACE-SC improves accuracy over plain Self-Consistency by 2.6%/0.9% on MathQA/ARC_C with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 3.3%/0.8% with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, demonstrating a gap between plain consistency (frequency) and calibrated confidence that confidence-weighted voting closes. GrACE-ES improves accuracy in all tested settings while substantially reducing the number of samples required (e.g. 38.6% of MathQA queries and 80.1% of the less-challenging ARC_C queries need only a single sample before the confidence threshold is reached), reaching accuracy comparable to or exceeding full-budget Self-Consistency at a much smaller expected sample count -- Table 3 shows GrACE-ES needs an average of only 2.14-4.48 samples on ARC_C/MathQA versus a fixed budget of 8, while achieving the best or near-best accuracy among all compared adaptive/non-adaptive TTS strategies. Comparing which confidence-elicitation method best drives adaptive TTS strategies (Table 3), GrACE consistently outperforms P(True) and Verbal confidence for both weighted self-consistency and early-stopping, with the least-calibrated method (P(True)) performing worst; overconfident verbalized scores are shown to cause premature termination on incorrect responses, while underconfident P(True) scores exhaust more of the sampling budget than necessary -- directly linking calibration quality to downstream TTS efficiency and reliability.
